title: No power, no internet: what to listen to
summary: The Henrico weather radio frequency and SAME code, plus AM/FM emergency stations and a car radio backup.

blocks.text: When the power and internet are out, **listening costs nothing, and you never transmit.** Start with a battery-powered NOAA Weather Radio, then AM/FM stations. Look up the exact frequencies on the Comms screen under Listen.

NOAA Weather Radio is a nationwide network of stations that broadcasts official warnings, watches and forecasts from your nearest National Weather Service office, 24 hours a day. It uses seven frequencies, and you need a special weather receiver or a scanner to hear it.

rows: The only transmitter in the sources we opened that explicitly lists Henrico. It began broadcasting June 21, 2024.
NWS lists it for the Piedmont region including the City of Richmond. The sources we opened do not name Henrico for it, so coverage is likely but not confirmed.

blocks.text: **Try both frequencies at your house and keep whichever is stronger.** All weather radios cover the same seven channels: 162.400, 162.425, 162.450, 162.475, 162.500, 162.525 and 162.550 MHz. Older radios that receive only three of them will not work everywhere.
SAME code: get alerts for your county only

**SAME** (Specific Area Message Encoding) lets a weather radio wake up and sound an alarm only for the counties you choose. A SAME code has six digits. The first digit is 0 for a whole county, and the other digits identify the state and county. Henrico County is **051087**. Follow your radio's manual to enter it.
If family live nearby, the same notice lists City of Richmond 051760, Hanover 051085, Charles City 051036 and New Kent 051127.
Pick a radio with all three: a tone alarm, SAME, and battery power. NWS says the tone alert is the most useful feature, because the radio can stay quiet until a watch or warning comes.

Program only your county. NWS warns that if you tune to a louder station that is not a SAME channel, you will not get the alerts. The usual range is roughly 40 miles from the transmitter, and terrain, your radio and its antenna change that.
These stations are named in Virginia's state Emergency Alert System (EAS) plan for the Richmond area. Any battery or car radio can receive them.

rows: Listed as the Richmond area's LP-1 station in the state plan.
Listed as LP-2. It is also a national primary EAS station.
Listed as LP-3. A news/talk station, and the one most likely to carry storm coverage. Also heard on 96.1 FM.

blocks.text: A car radio receives the same AM and FM stations, so it is a backup if your portable radio fails. Park outdoors first. Read the carbon monoxide guide (co-safety) before you run an engine for any reason.
The sources we opened give no battery-life numbers for weather radios, so check your radio's manual. What they do say:

items: Choose a weather radio that can run on batteries, usually one with an AC adapter and a battery compartment.
Use SAME and the tone alarm so the radio can sit quietly instead of playing all day.
Ready.gov says to plan for batteries and other backup power, such as a portable charger or power bank.

blocks.text: Weather radio is receive-only, so there is nothing to transmit and no license to worry about. For radios you can talk on, see the guide on what you are allowed to transmit.
